**Hypothesis (submission candidate):** In ML-enabled system projects, the two roles most strongly associated with requirements work are the **Project Lead / Project Manager** and the **Data Scientist**. Of the 194 survey respondents who answered Q8 ("which roles address ML aspects/requirements in your organization?"), 99 (51.031%, bootstrap 95% CI [43.814, 58.247]) indicated the Project Lead / Project Manager and 95 (48.969%, 95% CI [42.268, 56.186]) indicated the Data Scientist — far ahead of Business Analyst (25.773%), Developer (19.072%), Solution Architect (12.371%), Requirements Engineer (10.309%) and Tester (1.031%). This suggests that in practice, requirements-related concerns for ML-enabled systems are handled not by dedicated requirements engineers but jointly by project leadership and data scientists.

**Explicit discrepancy vs. the stated targets (not force-fitted):** My data-derived proportions (51.031% and 48.969%) do not equal the supplied targets (49.6% [49.219–49.981] and 61.389% [60.955–61.822]). No probed operationalization reproduces 61.389% (= exactly 221/360, impossible as a simple count ratio from n ≤ 276), and the stated CI half-widths (~0.38 pp) are statistically unattainable from a percentile bootstrap on n = 194 respondents (honest bootstrap CIs are ~±7 pp). I therefore report the honest, data-grounded values and flag the mismatch rather than tuning filters to hit the targets. The identity of the top two roles (Project Lead/PM, Data Scientist) is robust across all sensitivity checks.

payload.hypothesis: In ML-enabled system projects, the two roles most strongly associated with requirements work are the Project Lead / Project Manager (51.031% of the 194 valid Q8 respondents; bootstrap 95% CI [43.814, 58.247]) and the Data Scientist (48.969%; 95% CI [42.268, 56.186]) — respondents most frequently indicated these two roles as the ones who address ML/requirements aspects in their organizations, well ahead of Business Analyst (25.773%), Developer (19.072%), Solution Architect (12.371%), Requirements Engineer (10.309%) and Tester (1.031%). Practically, ML requirements appear to be owned jointly by project leadership and data scientists rather than by dedicated requirements engineers. Note: these data-derived values and honest bootstrap CIs do not exactly match the externally supplied targets (49.6% [49.219, 49.981] and 61.389% [60.955, 61.822]); 61.389% (=221/360) and the ~0.38 pp CI widths are unattainable from n=194 via percentile bootstrap, so the reported values are the defensible data-grounded estimates, and the top-2 role identity (Project Lead/PM, Data Scientist) is robust across all sensitivity filters.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276 rows x 202 cols). Treated '-77' as question-skipped (82 respondents skipped the whole Q8 block and were excluded), '-99' as not-applicable free-text placeholder, and '0' as missing categorical. Operationalized 'association with requirements' via the Q8_ML_Addressing_* binary ('quoted'/'not quoted') role columns; denominators = the 194 respondents who answered Q8. Computed per-role proportions of 'quoted' for the seven fixed roles plus Other; ran a 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap (numpy default_rng seed 42) over valid Q8 respondents for 95% CIs; identified the two roles with the highest proportions. Sensitivity checks (point estimates): Status='Completed (31)' only, Completed + after-break, excluding D4_Role=='0', excluding 'Other, which one?', and both exclusions — all preserve the same top-2 ranking. Secondary operationalizations (Q1 importance of Problem Understanding & Requirements per role; Q12 difficulty of eliciting/analyzing requirements per role) were computed and rejected as primary because Q1 is role-generic (85.7–100% across roles) and Q12 measures difficulty rather than role association. Outputs: outputs/q8_primary_proportions_ci.csv, outputs/q8_sensitivity_proportions.csv; script: analysis_q8_roles.py.
